Before you start#

Part I of the paper contains no theorem about geometry. It builds a dictionary of 32,000 concepts, asks which ones three tasks use, and looks at where concepts fire. Everything in parts II and III reuses this dictionary.

How to read this page#

Each section starts with a one-line summary, then quotes the paper in a paper box (with the page of the arXiv v3 PDF) and decodes it. Figures of the paper are followed by a "How to read this figure" box. Our own remarks are in Our reading boxes and are developed on page 6. Every number that is not in the paper is computed by checks/check_03.py.

The story of the page in seven steps#

  1. Hypothesis. A token activation is a sparse non-negative combination of a few unit "atoms" among 32,000 (§2, Def. 1).
  2. Dictionary. A stable (archetypal) sparse autoencoder gives codes Z and atoms D with A≈ZD.
  3. Importance. A linear probe W on A becomes a probe W′=DW⊤ on the codes; the score of concept i for output j is E[Zi​]Wij′​.
  4. Tasks. Classification uses many concepts, segmentation and depth few; the top concepts of a task are mutually aligned and span a low-dimensional subspace (Figs. 2, 3).
  5. What they look like. "Elsewhere" concepts for classification, border concepts for segmentation, monocular cues for depth (Figs. 4–6).
  6. Token types. Some concepts fire only on one kind of token: position-specific, cls-only, register-only (Figs. 7, 8).
  7. Hand-over. The statistics of Z and the geometry of D are the subject of page 4.

What you need#

  • The model, tokens, registers: ViT, registers, attention.
  • Sparse autoencoders and archetypal SAEs: SAE, archetypal SAE; the LRH itself: LRH.
  • Coherence of a dictionary: Gram matrix and coherence. UMAP, PCA, entropy, gradient × input, RISE: UMAP, PCA, entropy, grad × input, RISE.

1. The working hypothesis and how it is made operational#

The paper assumes that a token activation is a combination of at most k=8 non-negative multiples of unit vectors chosen among c=32,000 almost-orthogonal atoms, and finds those atoms with an archetypal sparse autoencoder trained on 1.4M images.

The problem#

A ViT has 768 neurons per token, but images contain far more than 768 things. Neurons are polysemantic: one neuron responds to several unrelated things. The paper's answer is to look for directions instead of neurons, and to ask that each activation uses only a few of them. This is the linear representation hypothesis (LRH), whose roots (superposition) are recalled on page 1.

Definition 1 — Linear Representation Hypothesis §2 · p. 5

A representation a∈Rd satisfies the LRH if there exist a sparsity constant k, an overcomplete dictionary D=(d1​,…,dc​)∈Rc×d and a coefficient vector z∈Rc such that a=zD, under the conditions:

(i) c≫d,(ii) μ(D)≡i=jmax​​Di​Dj⊤​​≤ε,  ∥Di​∥2​=1,(iii) ∣supp(z)∣≤k≪c.
a=zD
row-vector convention: a and z are rows, D has one atom per row. So a=∑i​zi​Di​, a combination of atoms.
(i) c≫d
overcompleteness: more atoms than dimensions (c/d≈41.7 here). It allows one atom per concept rather than one per dimension. A consequence is that the atoms cannot be orthogonal and the decomposition a=zD is not unique (see the toy example below).
(ii) μ(D)≤ε
quasi-orthogonality: the coherence μ is the largest absolute cosine between two different atoms (unit norm). Small ε means that atoms interfere little, so a sparse code can be read back from a. Recall: Gram matrix and coherence. The definition does not give a value of ε.
(iii) ∣supp(z)∣≤k≪c
sparsity: at most k non-zero codes. This is what makes the decomposition meaningful despite overcompleteness.

The paper motivates (ii) by compression: arranging c directions with minimal coherence is the problem of spherical codes (Tammes, Thomson), formalised by Grassmannian frames (Welch bound and Grassmannian frames). Definition 1 does not require non-negative codes: the non-negativity Z≥0 comes later, with the SAE.

A worked example by hand#

Example — d=2, three atoms, one active code

Take c=3 unit atoms in R2: D1​=(1,0), D2​=(0,1), D3​=(1,1)/2​. The off-diagonal entries of DD⊤ are 0, 0.7071, 0.7071, so μ(D)=0.7071. Overcomplete (3>2) but far from "quasi-orthogonal": a toy example cannot be both, since in the plane three directions have at least coherence 0.5 (the Welch bound (c−d)/(d(c−1))​=0.5; for the real dictionary it is 0.0356).

Take the code z=(1.5,0,2), with support size 2≤k. Then

a=zD=1.5(1,0)+2(0.7071,0.7071)=(2.9142, 1.4142).
Non-uniqueness: the same a is also z′=(2.9142,1.4142,0), a code on atoms 1 and 2 only. Both have support size 2. Sparsity alone does not choose between them; the SAE's encoder and its objective do.

The optimisation problem#

The factorisation problem §2 · p. 5

For a batch of n images, concatenating all tokens gives A∈Rnt×d. Find codes Z∈Rnt×c and a dictionary D∈Rc×d with

Z,Dmin​ ∥A−ZD∥F2​subject toZ≥0,  ∥Zi​∥0​≤k,  Di​∈conv(A).
∥A−ZD∥F2​
sum of squared reconstruction errors over all tokens: fidelity.
Z≥0
entrywise: concepts only add. A concept is "present with intensity zi​" and never "negatively present".
∥Zi​∥0​≤k
row i of Z (one token) has at most k non-zero entries. ∥⋅∥0​ counts non-zeros.
Di​∈conv(A)
each atom is a convex combination of real activations. This is the archetypal constraint: atoms stay inside the data cloud, which makes the dictionary stable across training runs (the paper's reason for choosing it). In practice conv(A) is replaced by the hull of 128,000 k-means centroids C and D=SC with S row-stochastic (non-negative rows summing to 1). Note that in Definition 1 the atoms are unit vectors; this problem does not state a normalisation. The paper does not say how the two are reconciled.
The exact configuration §2 · p. 5
768d: width of DINOv2-B
261t: 1 cls + 4 registers + 256 patches
32,000c: atoms
8k: active codes per token (BatchTopK)
128,000k-means centroids approximating conv(A)
1.4MImageNet-1k images, with augmentation
> 88%R2 of the reconstruction

Codes come from a single-layer encoder followed by a BatchTopK projection; training uses Adam for 50 epochs. So the dictionary is fitted on 1.4M×261≈3.65×108 tokens.

What these numbers say: each token, a point of R768, is rebuilt from 8 atoms (k/c=0.025% of the dictionary), and R2>88% means about 12% of the squared norm (after centring, as usual for R2; the paper does not say) is left unexplained. The R2 is the only fidelity number given.

What Z and D mean: statistics and geometry#

Interpretation of Z and D §2 · p. 5

Z encodes the statistical structure of the activation space: which concepts are active, how often, to what degree. D encodes the geometric structure: the atomic directions that span the space. The result is a library of 32,000 concept atoms, "each interpretable as a linear probe on DINOv2 activations".

This split organises the paper: page 3 (this one) uses Z and D together through a probe; page 4 studies Z (co-activation) and D (inner products) separately; page 5 replaces the linear picture. "Each atom is a linear probe" means: the score of atom i on a token is the inner product with Di​. Because the atoms are not orthogonal, this score is not the code zi​ the encoder produces.

One problem, five methods (App. B)#

Dictionary learning with method-specific constraints App. B · p. 33

(Z⋆,D⋆)=argmin∥A−ZD∥F2​ with, depending on the method, the constraints of the table.

MethodConstraint in the paperIn words
ACE — k-meansZi​∈{e1​,…,ek​}each token is assigned to one cluster; the atom is its centroid (one-hot code)
ICE — PCADD⊤=Iorthonormal atoms; at most d of them
CRAFT — NMFZ≥0, D≥0parts-based: both factors non-negative
AA — archetypal analysisZi​∈Δc, Di​∈conv(A)each token is a convex mix of archetypes that lie in the data hull
SAEZ=Ψθ​(A), ∥Z∥0​≤Kcodes come from an encoder Ψθ​ (TopK, JumpReLU, ReLU…); amortised, batched

Reading the table: moving down, constraints on Z go from "one atom" (k-means) to "few atoms" (SAE), and constraints on D from "orthonormal" to "inside the data". The paper's model combines the last two rows: an SAE encoder with archetypal atoms and non-negative sparse codes. The paper writes e1​,…,ek​ for the k-means row where one would expect the K cluster indicators; read k there as the number of clusters. In this appendix Δc is the simplex of Rc (simplex). Approaches trade fidelity ∥A−ZD∥F​ against sparsity ∥Z∥0​ along a Pareto frontier.

Our reading — what the definition leaves open

ε is never given a value, and Fig. 10 of the paper (page 4) shows inner products up to ±0.9 in the trained dictionary. So condition (ii) is a motivation, not a property verified for this dictionary. See page 6.

Why can the same activation have several valid codes in the toy example, and what chooses among them in practice?

Answer

With c>d the map z↦zD from Rc to Rd has a kernel, so many codes give the same a. In the example (1.5,0,2) and (2.9142,1.4142,0) both have two non-zeros. In practice the trained encoder Ψθ​ returns one code per token (the k largest after BatchTopK), so the choice is made by the architecture and the training objective.

2. Concept importance for a task#

A linear probe on activations is, in the concept basis, a linear probe on codes with weights W′=DW⊤; the importance of concept i for output j is its mean code times its weight, E[Zi​]Wij′​.

The problem#

The model has been trained on tasks (classification, segmentation, depth) through simple heads. We have 32,000 concepts. Which of them does a given head use? The head is linear, the concepts are linear directions, so the question can be answered exactly by one matrix product, with no new training.

Derivation#

Importance of concepts §3 · p. 6 and App. C.1 · p. 33

For a downstream prediction Y=AW⊤ with W∈Ro×d, o being the number of outputs, one has Y=(ZD)W⊤=ZW′ with W′=DW⊤. "This formulation provides a direct measure of each concept's importance through E(ZW′)=E(Z)W′, which represents the expected concept activation weighted by task-output alignment." In linear regimes this is "the optimal importance measure under standard faithfulness criteria (Theorem 3 in Fel et al. 2023)".

  1. Y=AW⊤ the probe: each row of A (one token) gives one row of Y (o scores). Shapes: (nt×d)(d×o)=nt×o.
  2. A≈ZD the dictionary reconstruction; Z is nt×c, D is c×d.
  3. Y≈ZDW⊤ substitute. Here the approximation sign hides the reconstruction error (A−ZD)W⊤, which the paper drops.
  4. Y≈Z(DW⊤)=ZW′ associativity. W′=DW⊤ has shape (c×d)(d×o)=c×o.
  5. Yn,j​=∑i=1c​Zn,i​Wij′​ write the product entry by entry: output j of token n is a sum over concepts of (code) × (weight). Only ≤k=8 terms are non-zero.
  6. E[Y⋅,j​]=∑i​E[Zi​]Wij′​ linearity of expectation (over tokens, and images). The i-th summand is the contribution of concept i to the mean output j: this is the score.
Wij′​=Di​⋅Wj​
alignment of atom i with the probe row j (the direction in activation space that raises output j). Large and positive: using concept i pushes output j up.
E[Zi​]
mean code of concept i: frequency × typical intensity (including zeros, since the code is 0 when the concept is off).
E[Zi​]Wij′​
importance of concept i for output j; a signed number.
Reminder — why "gradient × input"

For a function f and an input x, gradient × input attributes to coordinate i the number xi​∂f/∂xi​ (more). Here f=Yj​ is, as a function of the codes, ∑i​zi​Wij′​: linear, so ∂Yj​/∂zi​=Wij′​ and gradient × input is zi​Wij′​. Averaging over tokens gives E[Zi​]Wij′​. So the score is gradient × input in the concept basis, averaged. For a linear function this also equals the Integrated Gradients with a zero baseline and the occlusion score (replace zi​ by 0); the paper states this in App. C.1. RISE (more) averages over random masks and for a linear model is proportional to it.

The optimality claim#

The paper claims (footnote, §3, and App. C.1) that in the linear case this score is the optimal attribution under three faithfulness criteria, citing Theorem 3 of Fel et al. 2023 ("A holistic approach to unifying automatic concept extraction and concept importance estimation"). We have not re-derived this theorem; the statement below is "according to the paper".

  • C-Deletion: remove concepts one by one, most important first, and track the drop of the output. A good importance score makes it fall fast.
  • C-Insertion: add concepts one by one, most important first, starting from an empty input. A good score makes it rise fast.
  • C-μFidelity: correlation, over random subsets of concepts, between the sum of importances of the removed concepts and the actual change of the output.

The paper says that "in linear cases, these metrics coincide and share the same optimal attribution function". Intuition: if the output is ∑i​zi​Wij′​, removing a set S changes it by exactly ∑i∈S​zi​Wij′​, so the score is exactly additive, and ordering by it is optimal.

A worked example#

Example — three concepts, two outputs

Let E[z]=(0.5,0.2,0.05) and

W′=​20.5−3​−114​​(rows: concepts, columns: outputs).
Scores E[Zi​]Wij′​: concept 1: (1.00,−0.50); concept 2: (0.10,0.20); concept 3: (−0.15,0.20). Sums over concepts: (0.95,−0.10), which is the mean output E[Y] (the 2-vector).

Output 1 is driven by concept 1 (1.00 of 0.95; the others sum to −0.05). Output 2 is a near-cancellation: −0.5+0.2+0.2=−0.1. Concept 3 has the largest weights (−3,4) but a small mean code (0.05), so it ends up equal to concept 2 in output 2 and weaker than concept 1 everywhere. Weight alone does not make a concept important; frequency × intensity matters. Play with it:

Interactive figure (needs JavaScript).

What to look at: set E[Z3​] to 0 and see its bars vanish whatever W′; push all three alignments to the same sign on one output and see the contributions pile up; the black marker (sum of bars) is always the mean output.

What the definition leaves unclear#

Pitfalls
  • Two readings of ϕ. App. C.1 defines ϕ=E(Z)W′∈Ro, "the concept-importance vector for the probe". Summed over concepts this is the mean output (a vector of length o), not a vector of 32,000 scores. The per-concept score is each summand E[Zi​]Wij′​; the appendix says it "can be read from E(Z) together with the corresponding rows of W′".
  • Aggregation over outputs is not specified. The scores form a c×o matrix. To rank concepts for a task one needs one number per concept: the paper does not say whether it takes a sum, a max, an absolute value or the score of one class. (For a segmentation head with many classes, or depth with a regression output, the choices differ.)
  • Sign. With a signed score, "most important" may mean most positive or largest in absolute value. Not specified.
  • What is dropped. Reconstruction error (A−ZD)W⊤ (about 12% of the variance) and the probe's bias term are left out.
  • Tokens vs images. The score is an expectation over tokens. The classifier head of DINOv2 takes the concatenation of the cls token and the mean of the patch tokens (App. C.2), so a class score is not a function of one token. The averaging makes the token-level linear decomposition valid for the mean-pooled part, but the cls branch is a separate input.
  • Expectation includes zeros. E[Zi​] small can mean "rare but strong" or "frequent but weak"; the score cannot tell them apart.
Our reading — importance is not necessity

E[Zi​]Wij′​ measures a linear contribution to the logit; it says nothing about whether the model would still classify correctly without the concept, since other atoms are correlated with it. See page 6.

Reflex

When you see "importance of a concept for a linear probe" → push the probe through the dictionary, W′=DW⊤, then weight by the mean code.

3. What each task uses#

Classification draws on many concepts spread over the dictionary; segmentation and depth draw on few, compact groups; and the top-100 concepts of a task are more aligned with each other than random atoms, with a spectrum that decays faster.

The problem#

Once every concept has an importance score per task (previous section), one can ask whether tasks share concepts, how many they need, and whether the concepts they need form a recognisable region. The three tasks are read off the labels of Fig. 2: image classification (ImageNet-1k), semantic segmentation (ADE20K) and monocular depth (NYU Depth v2). The paper does not describe the heads here beyond "linear probes"; the classifier works on [cls, mean of patches] (App. C.2).

Different tasks recruit different concepts §3 · p. 6

"Figure 2 reveals that different tasks recruit different subsets of concepts, often with minimal overlap. Classification activates a wide and dispersed array of concepts, while segmentation and depth estimation draw on more compact and localized regions of the concept manifold. This may suggest functional regions in the latent space."

How to read this figure
  • Each dot is one atom of D; its position comes from UMAP (recall), which keeps neighbours close but distorts distances and areas. The same positions are used in all panels; only the colour changes (importance for the task).
  • What to look at: in the classification panel the important atoms are scattered over most of the map; in segmentation and depth they form compact patches.
  • What the authors conclude: functional regions; tasks reuse concepts non-uniformly.
  • What it does not show: UMAP clusters are not proof of low dimension, and the panels depend on the output dimension of each head (see below). The figure carries no number.
How to read this figure, panel by panel
  1. Left — histograms of importance (counts on a log axis). Classification scores run from about 1 to 4.3; segmentation from about 0.1 to 1.1; depth from 0 to about 0.25, with a sharp peak at 0. Order of magnitude reading from the plot, not exact. Depth has a spike of near-zero scores: most concepts are irrelevant for it. The caption says classification "utilizes a larger fraction of the dictionary", "likely reflecting the higher rank of the classification head". Note that the scales differ by a factor of 4 between tasks: scores are comparable within a task, not across tasks.
  2. Middle — cosine similarity of the top-100 concepts per task (kernel density), against all pairs. All pairs: a sharp peak at 0 (density about 9). Classification: peak near 0.01 with a right tail. Segmentation: peak shifted to about 0.07, tail to 0.6. Depth: bimodal, a mode near −0.08 and a shoulder at 0.1–0.25. Two tasks have atoms that point in similar directions (positive cosines); depth has also anti-aligned ones. Reference: for 100 random directions in R768 cosines have standard deviation 1/768​=0.036, whose Gaussian density peak is ≈11; the paper's all-pairs peak (about 9) is a little lower, i.e. the real dictionary is a bit broader than random.
  3. Right — Gram eigenvalues of the 100 top atoms, normalised to sum to 1, log scale, first 50 indices. The tasks start at 0.11–0.16 and fall to about 0.003–0.004; the random subset starts at about 0.047 and falls to about 0.009. A flat spectrum (100 orthogonal directions) would be 1/100=0.01 everywhere; one direction would give 1. So 0.11–0.16 means one direction carries 11–16% of the energy. Script check: 100 random unit vectors in R768 give a top value of about 0.018 and a minimum about 0.004 (Marchenko–Pastur), so even Gaussian directions are not exactly flat; the real random subset (0.047) is much steeper than that, because the dictionary is not isotropic (its own singular values decay, page 4).

What "low-dimensional functional subspace" means#

The paper's claim: the 100 atoms most used by a task nearly lie in a subspace of small dimension. Quantitatively, if the normalised Gram eigenvalues are λ1​≥λ2​≥… with ∑λl​=1, a fast decay means that a few directions carry most of the energy of these atoms. "Functional" refers to the task that selects them. It is a statement about 100 selected atoms, not about the task's weight vectors.

Appendix D · Fig. 19 App. D · p. 37

The top-500 concepts per task, and a random subset of 500, are projected by 2-D PCA: classification concepts are "broadly scattered", segmentation concepts "trace a coherent low-dimensional arc", depth shows "clear bimodal structure", the random subset "no discernible structure".

How to read this figure

Four scatter plots, each a PCA (recall) of its own 500 atoms: the axes are the two top principal directions of that subset, so shapes are compared, not positions. What to look at: scatter (classification), arc (segmentation), two groups (depth, echoing the bimodal cosine density of Fig. 3), blob (random). What it does not show: a 2-D PCA of 500 points of a 768-dimensional space can show an arc even if the variance in the other directions is large; the percentage of variance explained is not given. The bimodality of depth is later matched to the families of Fig. 6.

Caveats to keep in mind
  • The output dimension differs across probes. The classification head has one row per class, so more outputs, so more chances for a concept to score high on some output; the paper itself attributes the breadth to "the higher rank of the classification head". Comparing "how many concepts" across tasks therefore partly compares heads. How scores are merged over outputs is not stated (section 2).
  • Top-100 and top-500 are fixed cut-offs. Cosines and spectra are computed on a selection made by the importance score; a selection by any score tends to pick related atoms.
  • UMAP and PCA pictures are visual; the quantitative support is Fig. 3 middle and right.
  • The random baseline is not flat. A fair reference for "decays fast" is the random subset (0.047 to 0.009), not the flat line 0.01. Even the random subset's first eigenvalue is 4.7 times the flat value.
Our reading

The three panels agree with each other, but none compares with a task-independent selection of 100 atoms chosen to be correlated with each other (for instance neighbours of one atom). That control is the natural one to separate "task-specific" from "any selection of mutually similar atoms". See page 6.

4. "Elsewhere" concepts#

Some of the most important concepts for an ImageNet class fire on tokens that are not on the object, and only when the object is somewhere in the image: a concept map and a causal map of the same concept point at different places.

The problem#

Concept heat maps colour the tokens where a concept is active, and readers take this to mean "the concept is about this region". That assumption is not guaranteed. In a ViT, a token's activation depends on all other tokens through attention (recall), so a token can carry information about something located elsewhere.

"Elsewhere" concepts §3 · p. 7 and App. C.2 · p. 34

"Across a wide range of ImageNet classes, the top few most important concepts typically include not only interpretable objects or object-parts, but also an 'Elsewhere' concept": these "activate broadly across the tokens, but crucially not on the object itself", yet "their firing depends on the object's presence, and vanish if the object is removed". They express "not the object, but the object exists". They warn that heat maps "violate the unspoken assumption: the concept is just about the token where the concept fires".

How to read this figure
  • Token map (middle row): colour where the concept's code Zi​ is large, per patch. For these concepts the colour is on the surroundings and avoids the animal.
  • RISE map (bottom row): colour where masking the image changes the concept's activation. It lights up the animal itself.
  • The two maps disagree: where the concept fires is not what it depends on. That is the whole point.
  • Not shown: how many concepts are of this type (the paper says "recurring" and "for several classes"), and no number quantifies the effect; the object-removal claim is visual.

The RISE formula, decoded#

Causal attribution App. C.2 · p. 34
ΓRISE(i)​(f,x)=Em∼Pm​​(f(x⊙m)∣mi​=1)

f is "the composition of the model and the SAE", with 8000 forward passes per explanation.

m
a random binary (or soft) mask of the image, drawn from a distribution Pm​; ⊙ multiplies it pixel-wise with the image x, hiding the parts where m=0.
f(x⊙m)
here: the activation of the concept of interest on the masked image (the concept is the output of model + SAE).
mi​=1
conditioning on pixel (or region) i being visible.
Γ(i)
average concept activation over the masks that keep location i. If keeping i is what the concept needs, the average is high. Recall RISE. Estimated with 8000 masks.

Reading the logic: the object region gets a high Γ, because masks that hide the object kill the concept even if they keep the places where it fires. The paper's conclusion: "the object or animal itself is the most causally important region responsible for concept firing, even though the concept manifests its activation in spatially disjoint locations".

Interactive figure (needs JavaScript).

What to look at: toggle the object: the object concept and the Elsewhere concept both vanish, the background concept does not. Compare the "where it fires" row with the "what it depends on" row.

Why this is possible and useful#

  • Attention makes it possible. A patch token far from the object can read the object through attention and copy a summary of it into its own residual stream, so its activation encodes "the object is somewhere in the image".
  • Pooling makes it useful. The classifier takes cls and the mean of the patch tokens. A mean does not care where the evidence sits: class evidence spread over off-object tokens still reaches the logit. The paper adds that this can improve robustness to occlusion and viewpoint (App. C.2), a plausibility argument that it does not test.
  • Implication for heat maps. A concept's token map shows where it is expressed, not what it is about. The paper recommends combining localisation with causal perturbation.
Our reading — what is established

The figure shows a few examples from three classes. The paper's statements "implicitly learns a form of fuzzy spatial logic" and "fundamental computational strategy" go beyond that: no frequency of Elsewhere concepts, no random-concept control and no ablation of such a concept on the class score is given. The simplest alternative explanation of the token maps is a concept that reads global context from the registers or cls token. Page 6.

Reflex

When you see a concept heat map → ask where it fires and what it depends on; the two can be disjoint.

5. Segmentation uses border concepts#

All of the 50 most important concepts for segmentation fire along object contours, whatever the object, and form one tight cluster in the UMAP of atoms.

Segmentation and border concepts §3 · p. 7–8

"For segmentation, we observe that all the concepts among the top-50 consistently localize along object contours or spatial boundaries ... the precise visual features vary across classes (animal ears, tower edges, sea urchin spines), the spatial footprints remain strikingly consistent. In the concept embedding space, these border concepts form a visibly tight cluster."

How to read this figure
  • Overlays: colour is the concept's activation per token, on the image. Look at where: along limbs, heads, domes and rooflines, i.e. at silhouettes.
  • Right panel: the UMAP of atoms; the border concepts sit together.
  • Numbers: top-50; cosine and spectrum statistics are in Fig. 3 (segmentation: cosine peak near 0.07, tail to 0.6; top eigenvalue about 0.1–0.16) and Fig. 19 (an arc).
  • Not shown: that the 51st concept is not a border concept, and how the visualised examples were selected. The statement "all top-50" rests on the authors' inspection.

Intuition (ours, not the paper's): a segmentation head must assign a label to every patch, and the hardest patches are at boundaries; a "narrow, outline-shaped" footprint needs the token to know it is next to something else. The paper concludes that DINOv2 "allocates a dedicated region of its representational geometry to encoding object boundaries". "Dedicated region" is supported by the cluster (UMAP, Fig. 5) and by the higher cosines and faster spectral decay (Fig. 3), both for the top-100 and not the top-50.

Our reading

Border concepts and Elsewhere concepts are opposite cases of the same lesson on heat maps: here the map is the explanation (concepts are local), there it is not.

6. Depth uses monocular cues#

Perturbing images in five controlled ways and looking at how the top depth concepts react sorts them into three families — projective geometry, shadows, local frequency transitions — with many concepts in between.

The problem#

DINOv2 is trained without depth labels, yet linear probes predict depth well (the paper cites several works). What in its features supports this? The method: take the concepts that matter most for the depth probe, change the image so as to destroy one kind of depth cue at a time, and record how much each concept's activation drops. A concept's vector of five sensitivities is its profile.

Depth and monocular cue concepts §3 · p. 8 and App. C.3 · p. 35

Five manipulations: "local median blurring to suppress shadows, global blur to remove fine details, high-pass filtering to emphasize geometric patterns, soft edge enhancement to retain contours, and geometric warping to distort perspective cues". The profiles are projected with UMAP and give "three coherent clusters": projective geometry (perspective lines, structural convergence), shadow-based (soft lighting gradients), local frequency transitions (abrupt changes of detail or texture). "This taxonomy is not exhaustive: some concepts exhibit mixed sensitivity profiles."

PerturbationWhat it removes or keeps (per the paper)
Local median blursmall-scale texture and lighting detail; "to suppress shadows" (main text)
Global blurfine detail, high spatial frequencies
High-pass filterkeeps edges and lines, removes smooth shading: "emphasizes geometric patterns"
Soft edgeskeeps contours (edge-preserving)
Warpingdistorts perspective geometry
How to read this figure
  • Top strip: an indoor scene and a vaulted ceiling under (Original), Local Median, Blur, High pass, Soft Edges, Warping.
  • Bar charts (y: 0 to 1, how much the activation is affected; bars in the order median, blur, high-pass, soft edges, warping; values read off the plot, approximate): Local frequency transition: 0.57, 0.52, 0.06, 0.03, 0.1 — sensitive to median and blur only. Projective: 0.25, 0.25, 0.65, 0.38, 0.1 — peak at high-pass, then soft edges. Shadow: 0.07, 0.45, 0.12, 0, 0.07 — peak at blur.
  • Illustrations: frequency: blurred-background sports shots (depth-of-field); projective: spiral staircases and shells (converging lines); shadow: weight-lifting in a gym (lighting gradients).
  • UMAP: about five visible groups of dots, not exactly three.
  • Not shown: how many of the top concepts fall in each family. The bars are one example per family.
The text and the figure disagree on two details

App. C.3 says that the projective cluster "shows sensitivity to warping and high-pass" and the shadow cluster "primary sensitivity to median filtering". In Fig. 6 the projective bars show warping at only about 0.1, and the shadow bars peak at blur, not at median. We follow the figure; the appendix wording looks like an error. The main text also says median blurring is used "to suppress shadows", yet it is the frequency family that responds to it, and the shadow family responds to global blur.

Fig. 18: the full set#

How to read this figure

Each panel is titled by a concept id; five bars on a 0–1 axis in the order of Fig. 6. Profiles of the three families appear (a single high bar at blur; high at the first two; high at the middle), but many panels have two or three bars of similar height, a few are nearly flat and high (all bars around 0.8–1, e.g. in row 4 and row 5), and a few respond only to warping. The panels are small and the labels hard to read. This is the evidence behind "many concepts exhibit mixed sensitivity profiles". The caption's "systematically organized" is not quantified: no count per family is given.

Link with classical cues. The appendix says the taxonomy "aligns with classical monocular depth cues from visual neuroscience": linear perspective and convergence (projective), shading and shadows, and blur / texture gradients (defocus and frequency). Names only: the paper does not test the link to human perception, and does not cite a particular source here.

Our reading

Perturbations are not clean: a high-pass filter also removes shading and a blur also removes edges, so a profile cannot identify a single cue; the families are best read as "kinds of image statistic". The "three clusters" are the authors' labelling of the UMAP. Page 6.

7. Token-type-specific concepts#

Where on the 261 tokens does a concept fire, on average? Most concepts are spread out; a tail is localised (a position, the cls token, or the four registers), and the register-only ones encode global scene properties.

The problem#

A ViT has three kinds of token (tokens): 256 patches tied to places, one cls token and four registers that read and write global information. Are some concepts reserved for one kind?

The footprint and its entropy#

Footprint §4 · p. 9 and App. G · p. 39

Reshape Z as a tensor Rn×t×c. For concept i the footprint is

ωi​=N1​n=1∑N​Zn,:,i​∈Rt.
"Zn,:,i​ is the concept map (a vector of 261 scalars) of concept i on input n." The paper then measures "the entropy of its empirical footprint distribution": low entropy, localised; high entropy, "spatially uniform".

Zn,:,i​
the 261 codes of concept i on image n: 1 for cls, 4 for registers, 256 for patches.
ωi​
their average over N images: the mean activation of the concept at each token position (a 16×16 map plus 5 special values).
entropy
To be an entropy, ωi​ must be turned into a probability vector, pl​=ωi,l​/∑l′​ωi,l′​, then H=−∑l​pl​lnpl​ (recall). The paper does not write this normalisation or the logarithm base; the range of Fig. 7 (up to about 5.5) fits natural logarithms, ln261=5.565.

Reference values, computed by checks/check_03.py for footprints that are uniform on a set of m tokens (then H=lnm):

FootprintmH=lnm (nats)
one token (e.g. cls only)10
the four registers41.386
the five special tokens51.609
one grid column162.773
left third of the grid (5 columns × 16 rows)804.382
a third of the 261 tokens874.466
the 256 patches2565.545
all 261 tokens2615.565

Also, if half the mass is on the registers and half uniform on patches, H=4.159. The maximum ln261=5.565 is hardly smaller than ln256=5.545: the entropy hardly sees the five special tokens, a concept that is uniform on patches and absent on specials is at 5.545. eH can be read as an effective number of tokens.

Interactive figure (needs JavaScript).

What to look at: use the presets; note how a footprint covering a third of the image is already at 4.4, and how long the bulk of the histogram of Fig. 7 (4–5.5) is: "high entropy" means "not confined to a small region", which includes concepts with a clear but broad preference (left/right, centre).

Fig. 7: the histogram and the bar chart#

How to read this figure
  • Histogram (x: entropy 0–5.5; y: number of concepts, log). A spike at 0 of about 110 concepts (single-token footprints), a sparse scatter of 1–10 concepts per bin between 0.3 and 3, then a rise to the bulk: at 4 about 30–100 per bin, at 5 about 103, peak around 5.2–5.5 with several thousand per bin. Compare with the table above: 0 is a single token, 4–4.5 is a third of the image, the bulk is "nearly uniform".
  • Token maps (16×16 patch grid, colour = mean activation). Low entropy: a single blob, a vertical or horizontal strip, a border. Medium: a region (centre, left, bottom). High: nearly flat, with texture.
  • Not shown: the special tokens (maps show patches only), and which entropy cut defines "low".
  • A footprint with all its mass on one token has H=0; on the four registers equally, H=1.386. So the spike at 0 means single-token concepts (for instance cls-only, or one fixed patch); register-only concepts, which spread over four tokens, would sit at or below 1.386, in the sparse part of the histogram. The paper does not say which bins hold them.

The three categories#

Footprint types §4 · p. 9–10
  1. Position-specific concepts on narrow regions ("left-only", "bottom-only"): "residual positional encoding, biases in the training data, or local geometric primitives".
  2. A unique cls-only concept that fires "persistently on the cls token across all images", "closely tied to the positional embedding of the cls token", maybe an "ID" or "passport".
  3. reg-only concepts: a "much more diverse" group, whose variety "cannot be explained by position alone", encoding "non-spatial features".
Remark — "one" or "about 30"?

The text (§4, App. G, caption of Fig. 21) says a single concept is cls-only. The bar chart, on a log axis, shows a cls-only bar at about 30, a reg-only bar at about 150 and a spatial-only bar at about 3×104 (≈ 31.8k reading the figure). Both cannot be true with the same definition of "only". The paper does not define the threshold for "exclusively". The order of magnitude of "hundreds" for registers is roughly matched (about 150). We cannot resolve this from the paper.

Fig. 8: what register-only concepts are about#

How to read this figure

Each concept is shown by images that maximally activate it; there is no token map, since the concept is not about a place. What they have in common is global: motion blur, lighting and shadows, caustic reflections, wide-angle warping or depth of field, and artistic or rendering style. Authors: registers act as "a conduit for abstract scene-level information". Not shown: how these concepts were chosen among the hundreds, and whether they matter for any task of section 2. Link with the registers' purpose: registers were added to ViTs to hold global computation instead of letting patch tokens be hijacked for it; here the concepts they host are global properties, consistent with that purpose.

Fig. 21 and Fig. 20 (App. G)#

How to read this figure
  • Left: the colour is the mean total activation per token (scale about 7 to 12). Patches are about 9–10, with a bright bottom half and a darker top centre. In the last row the five special tokens sit apart: two registers at the top of the scale (about 11 to 12), the others near the bottom (about 7), cls in the middle (about 9.5). The caption says "elevated activity on register and cls tokens", which is only true of some of them as we read the picture. The unit is not stated (we read it as the sum over concepts of the code, per token).
  • Middle: patches only, scale 8.8–10.4: high on the left and right sides of the lower half, low at top centre. A "subtle positional bias".
  • Right: same bar chart as Fig. 7 right, and same mismatch with the text.

Fig. 20 (p. 39) is a very large image: the average maps of 2,500 concepts sorted by entropy, from localised strips and blobs at the top to uniform maps at the bottom. It illustrates the continuum of the histogram; we do not reproduce it.

Our reading

Two readings of the register-only concepts are compatible with the figure: registers hold global scene information (the paper's reading) or they are a place where the model stores attributes of the whole image that patch tokens also see weakly. The paper tests neither. See page 6.

8. Summary and reflexes#

Part I in ten lines
  1. Definition 1 (LRH): a=zD, with c≫d, unit atoms of low coherence, and at most k non-zero codes.
  2. Operationalised by an archetypal SAE: min∥A−ZD∥F2​, Z≥0, ∥Zi​∥0​≤8, Di​∈conv(A); d=768, t=261, c=32,000, 1.4M images, R2>88%.
  3. Z = statistics, D = geometry. ACE, ICE, CRAFT, AA and SAE are the same problem with different constraints (App. B).
  4. A probe W becomes W′=DW⊤ on codes; concept i has score E[Zi​]Wij′​ for output j (gradient × input in the concept basis; optimal in the linear case by Thm. 3 of Fel et al. 2023, according to the paper). The paper's ϕ=E(Z)W′ is the sum of these scores; aggregation over outputs and the dropped reconstruction error are not specified.
  5. Classification uses many concepts; segmentation and depth few (Figs. 2, 3 left). Top-100 concepts of a task are more aligned than random ones and have a faster-decaying Gram spectrum (Fig. 3, App. D, Fig. 19).
  6. "Elsewhere" concepts fire off the object but depend on it (Fig. 4, RISE with 8000 masks): where a concept fires is not what it is about.
  7. Segmentation: border concepts, one tight cluster (Fig. 5). Depth: projective, shadow and frequency families, many mixed (Figs. 6, 18).
  8. Footprint ωi​=N1​∑n​Zn,:,i​; its entropy runs from 0 (one token) to ln261=5.565; most concepts are near the top, about 110 at 0 (Fig. 7).
  9. Token-type concepts: position-specific, cls-only (text: one; bar chart: about 30), register-only (about 150), the latter about global scene properties (Fig. 8).
  10. Caveats stated by the paper: the depth taxonomy is not exhaustive; our own: evidence is visual and selected.
  • When you see a=zD → rows are tokens, atoms are rows of D, codes are non-negative and sparse.
  • When you see "importance for a linear probe" → W′=DW⊤, then E[Zi​]Wij′​; summing over i must give the mean output.
  • When you see a UMAP or a 2-D PCA of atoms → treat it as an illustration; look for the cosine or spectrum statistic that backs it.
  • When you see a spectrum on a log axis → compare with the flat value 1/n and with a random baseline.
  • When you see a concept heat map → ask what it depends on, not only where it fires.
  • When you see an entropy of a footprint → translate it as ln(effective number of tokens).

What the next page does with it. Page 4 keeps the same Z and D and studies their statistics (which concepts fire together, how often) and their geometry (inner products, singular values), then the shape of an image in the token space.

9. Exercises#

Exercise 1 — Shapes ★

With n images, t=261, c=32,000, d=768 and a head with o=1000 outputs, give the shapes of A, Z, D, W, W′, Y. How many non-zero codes does one image have at most?

Hint

Y=AW⊤ must be nt×o.

Solution

A: nt×768; Z: nt×32000; D: 32000×768; W: 1000×768; W′=DW⊤: 32000×1000 (32 million entries); Y: nt×1000. One image: 8×261=2088 non-zeros at most, out of 261×32000.

Exercise 2 — Toy dictionary ★

With the atoms of the toy example (D1​=(1,0), D2​=(0,1), D3​=(1,1)/2​), compute zD for z=(0,1,1). Does the dictionary satisfy condition (ii) for ε=0.1?

Solution

zD=(0,1)+(0.7071,0.7071)=(0.7071,1.7071). The coherence is max(0,0.7071,0.7071)=0.7071>0.1: condition (ii) fails. In R2 any three unit vectors have coherence at least 0.5 (the Welch bound), so no choice of atoms would work.

Exercise 3 — Importance ★★

Same W′ as in the worked example but E[z]=(0.4,0.1,0.5). Compute the score matrix and the mean outputs. Which concept is most important for output 1 and for output 2? What changed with respect to the example, and why?

Hint

Multiply each row of W′ by the matching mean code.

Solution

Scores: concept 1: (0.80,−0.40); concept 2: (0.05,0.10); concept 3: (−1.50,2.00). Sums: (−0.65,1.70). Concept 3 now dominates both outputs in absolute value (1.5 and 2.0), and the mean output 1 becomes negative. Its weights were already the largest; the mean code went from 0.05 to 0.5, ten times more. Importance is the product of frequency × intensity and alignment.

Exercise 4 — Gradient × input ★★

Show that E[Zi​]Wij′​ is the average of gradient × input of Yj​ with respect to the codes. Why does the equality fail for the true model (the SAE decoder is linear but the network is not)?

Solution

Yn,j​=∑i​Zn,i​Wij′​, so ∂Yn,j​/∂Zn,i​=Wij′​ and gradient × input is Zn,i​Wij′​; averaging over n gives E[Zi​]Wij′​. For a non-linear function of the codes (for instance a later transformer layer between the codes and the output), the gradient depends on the input and the average of products is not the product of averages. Here the probe is linear in A and the reconstruction A≈ZD is linear in Z, so only the reconstruction error breaks it.

Exercise 5 — Entropy of footprints ★

Compute the entropy (nats) of a footprint that is (a) equal on the five special tokens and zero on patches; (b) half on cls, half spread uniformly over the 256 patches.

Hint

Normalise to a probability vector first; H=−∑plnp.

Solution

(a) H=ln5=1.609. (b) H=−21​ln21​−256⋅5121​ln5121​=21​ln2+21​ln512=21​(0.693+6.238)=3.466. A single token that carries half the mass lowers the entropy by 2.1 nats from the 5.545 of the uniform patches.

Exercise 6 — A broad but biased concept ★★

A concept puts 80% of its footprint mass uniformly on 80 patches (the left third) and 20% uniformly on the other 176 patches, nothing on special tokens. Compute H and eH. Where in the histogram of Fig. 7 does it fall, and would the paper call it position-specific?

Solution

p=0.8/80=0.01 on 80 patches, p=0.2/176=0.001136 on 176. H=−0.8ln0.01−0.2ln0.001136=3.684+1.356=5.040, eH=154: as if the concept were uniform on 154 tokens. It lies in the bulk (between the orange and red boxes of Fig. 7), not in the "low-entropy" tail, though a clear left bias exists. High entropy does not mean "no position preference".

Exercise 7 — Reading the Gram spectrum ★★

The normalised Gram eigenvalues of 100 atoms sum to 1. (a) What is the flat value? (b) If the largest is 0.15 and the other 99 are equal, what is each, and what is eH of the spectrum (H=−∑λlnλ)? (c) Why is 0.15 not impossible for 100 atoms of mean cosine 0 pairwise?

Solution

(a) 1/100=0.01. (b) 0.85/99=0.00859 each; eH=75.8 "effective dimensions" out of 100. (c) Cosines averaging 0 do not mean a flat spectrum: a few strongly correlated pairs and many nearly orthogonal ones still give a top eigenvalue well above 0.01; and for 100 random directions of R768 the top is already about 0.018 (computed). The paper's 0.11–0.16 is about 15 times the flat value.

Exercise 8 — Why Elsewhere concepts help a pooled classifier ★★★

A classifier logit is the mean over 16 patch tokens of wzp​ for one concept with weight w=2. (a) The concept fires with code 1 on the 12 patches off the object. What is the logit contribution? (b) The same concept firing only on the 4 object patches? (c) Only 4 of the 12 off-object patches still fire (the rest are occluded). Explain what pooling does with locations, and what would break if the logit used one token only.

Hint

The mean is invariant under permutations of tokens.

Solution

(a) 2⋅12/16=1.5. (b) 2⋅4/16=0.5. (c) 2⋅4/16=0.5: the loss is proportional to the number of tokens that stop firing. The mean only counts how much evidence there is, not where; so a concept firing on the many off-object tokens contributes more than one on the few object tokens, as long as it fires on them. With one token only (the cls, say) location would matter: an off-object token could not use a concept whose evidence sits elsewhere unless attention carried it, which is precisely what the Elsewhere concepts show it does. Caution: this explains why such concepts can help; the paper does not measure that they do.
